content.text: The Dependency Inversion Principle is about which way source code dependencies point and who owns the abstraction between business policy and a detail. A DI container only wires objects together, and an interface extracted from every class usually copies the detail's shape instead of inverting anything. Put interfaces where policy meets a detail, shape them around what the policy needs, and keep the container at the edge.
Marketing wants order confirmations on WhatsApp as well as email. The solution looks like a SOLID textbook: every class has an
, because each one builds HTML and passes SMTP settings to
. There's an interface for everything, and the business code still depends on email.
The belief: applying the Dependency Inversion Principle means putting an interface in front of every class, registering each pair in a DI container, and receiving everything through constructors.
It's an understandable belief. ASP.NET Core ships with a container, and most tutorials pair
. The ideas really are related: Microsoft's architecture guide says "The practice of dependency injection is made possible by following the dependency inversion principle."

The half-truth: inversion does need an abstraction, and injection is a common way to deliver the implementation. But the container is plumbing, and counting interfaces tells you nothing about which way the dependencies point.
The principle is about direction and ownership

routine that reads from a keyboard and writes to a printer. Inverted,
as plain parameters. There's no container anywhere, and he even counts C's
as the same move: that version "still uses dependency inversion!"

Microsoft's guide puts the result in .NET terms: class A calls B at run time, while B depends "on an interface controlled by A at compile time". The interface belongs to the caller. Clean Architecture builds its whole layout on this idea; here we stay at the level of a single dependency.
So what should the abstraction look like? Martin describes high-level policy as "the truths that do not vary when the details are changed." In his button-and-lamp example, the abstraction isn't an
, because the policy is "to detect an on/off gesture from a user and relay that gesture to a target object." The lamp implements the button's interface, not the other way around.

Brett Schuchert, writing on Martin Fowler's site, shows the opposite case: injecting a JDBC connection into a Monopoly game is dependency injection, but at a level far below the game's domain. A board repository is the abstraction that fits.
Fowler names the two kinds of interface. A
"is defined by looking at a specific interaction between suppliers and consumers." A
mirrors one class, and, as he puts it, "With a header interface all you have to do is duplicate the public methods, no thought needed."
is the second kind: its methods still talk SMTP, so the order code still depends on the detail's shape, now with an
in front. His advice: "you should only use interfaces when you really need substitutability, and if you do need interfaces you should think hard about what the consumer of that interface needs."

Schuchert sums up the three terms in one line: "DI is about wiring, IoC is about direction, and DIP is about shape." Martin made the same point in 2010: "Dependency Injection is just a special case of Dependency Inversion," and it "doesn't require a framework; it just requires that you invert your dependencies and then construct and pass your arguments to deeper layers." His own preference, stated as such: "Most of the time the best kind of Dependency Injection to use, is the manual kind." A container saves you the
. It can't decide what your interfaces should say.
The fix: let the policy own a narrow interface

Microsoft's guide asks classes to state their collaborators in their constructors: the Explicit Dependencies Principle. Martin's complaint about Guice fits any container: "I don't want Guice to be poured all over my app."
Read an interface's method names and parameter types and ask whether they'd survive replacing the technology behind it.

blocks.title: Opinion: where interfaces earn their keep

content.text: This is our view, not a rule from the sources: interfaces pay off where policy reaches out to I/O, third-party services, the clock or randomness, and where you really have several implementations. Pure calculations, value objects and mappers rarely need one.
How to apply it in your project
List interfaces with exactly one implementation whose methods mirror that class. For each, ask whether it guards a real detail, such as I/O or a vendor, or just a class.

items.title: Rewrite boundary interfaces from the caller's side

content.text: Name the interface for what the business code needs, use domain types in its signatures, and move it next to the code that calls it. The old class becomes an adapter that implements it.

items.title: Drop interfaces in front of pure logic

content.text: Call calculators, policies and mappers directly, and test them directly. Keep an interface only where you need substitutability.
